newsitem.title: USA: Hughes rises as bidding war reported.
newsitem.headline: Hughes rises as bidding war reported.

text.p: Shares of Hughes Electronics soared Thursday on reports Northrop Grumman Corp. and Raytheon Co. were in a bidding war for the General Motors Corp. unit's missile and radar businesses valued at about $9 billion.
Raytheon reportedly has bid $9 billion for the businesses while Northrop Grumman was said to have offered as much as $500 million more, according to Thursday's Wall Street Journal.
None of the companies reportedly involved would comment.
"GM and Hughes have no comment on the speculation," GM spokeswoman Toni Simonetti said. Raytheon and Northrop Grumman officials also declined to comment.
Hughes Electronics shares, which trade separately from GM's stock, rose $1.75 to $62.875 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange while Raytheon and Northrop Grumman both fell.
Raytheon lost $1.75 to $47 and Northrop fell $1.50 to $77.75, both on the NYSE.
"I don't think it's necessarily the high bidder that will win," said Paul Nisbet, a defence analyst at JSA Research.
General Motors' desire to avoid a hefty tax bill and the comparative financial strength of Raytheon give it the edge, analysts said.
"It's more advantageous to Raytheon because it's larger and stronger financially (than Northrop)," Nisbet said.

Analysts said that to avoid paying about $2 billion of capital gains taxes resulting from a cash sale of Hughes, GM wants to load up Hughes with up to $5 billion in debt. Hughes has only $200 million of debt.
Stock of the acquiring company would make up the balance of the payment.

"For Northrop to issue $4 billion to $6 billion in stock they would actually have to issue enough stock to give a majority holding to General Motors, whereas Raytheon would have to give about 30 percent of their holdings (to GM)," Nisbet said.
He added that it was unlikely that GM would want to hold a majority interest in Northrop.
"It would seem to me that Raytheon can come in lower than Northrop and still get it," he said.
Northrop has about $3.3 billion in debt with $1.6 billion in shareholder equity.

Raytheon -- even after this week's agreement to buy Texas Instrument Inc'.s defence assets for $2.95 billion -- has about $6.5 billion of debt with about $4.6 billion in stockholder equity, making its debt load lighter relative to Northrop's.

Raytheon also could choose to sell off a non-defence business, such as its Engineers & Contructors unit, for more than $3 billion, thereby softening the heavy debt load that would come with Hughes, analysts said.
"I think Raytheon has the upper hand just because of that," said William Fiala, an analyst at brokerage firm Edward Jones. "Their options are almost limitless."
